summary: Tether is an offline-first health app that helps astronauts monitor themselves when the ground is far away. On Mars a message to the flight surgeon takes up to 20 minutes each way, so Tether tells the crew member what to do now. A one-minute daily check-in logs vitals, sleep and mood; explainable rules compare each value with clinical ranges and the person's own baseline and raise early warnings (for example a possible infection before a fever), always with clear next steps and when to contact the flight surgeon. It covers NASA's five hazards of spaceflight: radiation dose against NASA's 600 mSv career limit with live NASA DONKI space weather, isolation (mood, stress, NASA Cognition-style brain games), gravity (exercise plans by location, bone and nutrition tracking), distance (delayed messages and a one-tap report for the flight surgeon) and the closed habitat. A gamified routine, crew profiles and a mission control view keep the whole crew engaged. It works without internet, keeps data on the device and is available in six languages.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Tether is a self-assessment health app for crews on the ISS, the Moon, deep space and Mars. Far from Earth a flight surgeon cannot answer in real time (up to 20 minutes one way from Mars), so Tether turns each reading into a clear status (OK, Watch, Act), explains why, and says what to do now and when to contact the ground.

HOW IT WORKS

- Daily check-in in about a minute: heart rate (also from a Bluetooth sensor), blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep and mood, with step-by-step instructions for each measurement.

- Explainable, deterministic rules (no black-box AI): clinical ranges from AHA, ADA and CDC, a personal baseline (the crew member's own median), and early warnings from streaks, worsening trends, 7-day projections and combined patterns (possible infection, sleep debt, accumulated fatigue, exercise below plan). Every warning has a "Why am I seeing this?" and a master caution for anything that needs action.

- NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, each with its own status. Radiation: dosimeter log, mission and career dose against the NASA-STD-3001 600 mSv limit, expected dose rates by location from NASA, live NASA DONKI space weather, a NOAA S1-S5 solar storm simulator with a shelter drill, and a mission dose planner (station, Moon, Mars). Isolation: mood, stress check, a reaction self-test like the one used on the ISS, NASA Cognition-style brain games and 4-7-8 breathing. Gravity: exercise plans by location, nutrition and body mass. Distance: a report for the flight surgeon (copy, share, download or QR code) and a message outbox that shows the real signal delay. Hostile environment: a symptom guide with self-care and escalation levels.

- Body map, mission timeline (what to expect and when), and "Real crews": published NASA findings such as the Twins Study, Apollo and station crews, each linked to the screen that watches for it.

- Gamification and routine: a morning, midday and evening routine that only ticks off when a real measurement is logged, points, ranks, streaks, mission patches, a daily space quiz, a Veggie-inspired space garden, a journey map and shared crew goals.

- Crew: several profiles on one device, a mission control view of the whole crew, a shared medical kit with expiry and stock warnings, and use cases with demo crew members (infection, low mood, sleep deprivation, rising blood pressure, solar storm, skipped exercise, and a historical case rebuilt from Apollo 15).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It keeps working with no connection, keeps every reading on the device, and works in six languages used in human spaceflight (English, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Japanese and French). The same tool helps people far from a doctor on Earth: polar stations, submarines, offshore platforms, expeditions and remote rural areas.

TOOLS

React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, IndexedDB (Dexie), Zustand, Recharts, Motion, Lucide icons, a Progressive Web App (installable, offline), Vitest (185 automated tests), Web Bluetooth, and the NASA DONKI API. Deployed on Vercel. The demo video was built with HyperFrames.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

We chose explainable rules over an AI chatbot because a crew on Mars cannot rely on a network, and every number cites its source. Gamification only rewards real measurements, so points cannot be farmed. Every status uses an icon and a word, never colour alone. Demo data is always labelled as simulated.
